svg.title: Publishing the source of a private project, without the parts that must stay private — Publication keeps its safety promises from source selection to repeated releases
svg.text: Publishing the source of a private project, without the
Scenario: Publication keeps its safety promises from source selection to repeated releases
Source bytes that can be copied safely
Credentials and setup failures remain visible

g.text: Given an approved source file with a local smudge filter
The real Git repository contains an approved source file. A local smudge filter would
substitute uncommitted text during a checkout. These fixture contracts run the shipped tasks
against disposable repositories and a fixture approval API; the separate journey below uses
GitLab itself.
Then export keeps the committed bytes despite the local smudge filter
The export command must succeed, and the exported file must equal the committed bytes
exactly. The card reads that exported file.
Given an approved tracked source file also matched by its ignore file
Both .gitignore and src/message.txt are tracked and approved. The ignore pattern also
matches the source file.
Then publication includes every approved tracked path despite ignore
rules
The public Git tree and file contents must match the manifest. The card reads that tree and
the published blob.
Given an approved source path whose directory starts with a dash
The tracked and approved path is -public/message.txt. The leading dash is part of its name.
Then export preserves a path that starts with a dash
The export must succeed and preserve every byte. A directory name must not become an option
passed to a shell utility.
Given a candidate source entry that is a symbolic link
The Git index records src/host with symlink mode 120000. Its target is outside the
repository.
Then the dry run names and rejects the symbolic link
The dry run must return a failure and name src/host. No public commit may result from this
check.
Given a candidate source file that contains an LFS pointer
The committed source file contains a Git LFS pointer, whose blob is displayed here.
Then the dry run names and rejects the LFS pointer
The dry run must fail and name src/large.txt because the pointer is not the large file's
source content.
Given a source commit missing the framework denylist
The prepared commit deletes denylist.base. Git shows the deletion before the check runs.
Then the dry run refuses a missing framework denylist
The dry run must fail and name denylist.base. An absent framework safety floor is a
configuration error.
Given a Git blob reader that fails before scanning
The displayed test wrappers make Git cat-file blob exit 73 and record every scanner
invocation. The publication scan setting is required.
Then publication stops before scanning or pushing when export fails
The task must fail, the scanner invocation log must remain empty, and the public repository
must contain zero commits. These wrappers test failure ordering; they do not test scanner
detection.
Given a Git blob reader that fails after a successful scan
The Git reader works through export. The scanner fixture records success, then the reader
fails while the public index is being built. The displayed scripts define this exact fault.
Then publication stops before pushing when a post-scan blob read fails
A successful scan cannot turn a later read error into an empty published file. The scan log
has one entry and the public repository must still have zero commits.
Given a publication explicitly disabled at runtime
TASK_PUBLICATION_ENABLED is false in the task's actual environment.
Then disabled publication neither contacts the forge nor creates a
public commit
The task must report that publication is disabled, make zero fixture API calls, and leave
the public repository empty.
Given an automatic job environment configured for manual publication
This local fixture sets CI=true and TASK_PUBLICATION_ON=manual without CI_JOB_MANUAL. It
exercises the runtime guard; it is not a GitLab job.
Then an automatic job does not publish in manual mode
The command must exit successfully with a manual-mode explanation and leave zero public
commits.
Given a branch job environment configured for tag publication
This local fixture sets CI=true and TASK_PUBLICATION_ON=tag without CI_COMMIT_TAG.
Then a branch job does not publish in tag mode
The command must exit successfully and leave zero public commits. Actual job creation
remains part of GitLab CI configuration.
Given a locally available source ready for an offline check
The source ref and manifest are available in the local repository.
Then the dry run succeeds without contacting the forge
The dry run must succeed while the fixture API request log remains empty. Approval
verification happens when publishing.
Given an offline check whose source ref is absent locally
The requested ref is absent. The origin points to the local HTTP fixture so an attempted
fetch would be recorded.
Then the dry run refuses the absent ref without fetching it
The check must fail and make zero HTTP requests. Offline checking must not repair an absent
ref by accessing the network.
Given a publication given an unsupported scan-done flag
TASK_PUBLICATION_SCAN is set to done, the removed caller-controlled bypass.
Then publication refuses a caller assertion that scanning is done
The task must fail and leave zero public commits. The supported modes are required and off.
Given an owner-resolved discussion unrelated to publication
The fixture API returns an owner-resolved spelling discussion. Its actual response is shown
beside the manifest blob hash.
Then an unrelated discussion cannot approve publication
Publishing must fail and leave zero public commits. The owner's identity alone cannot turn
another discussion into publication approval.
Given an owner-resolved publication discussion for another manifest
The discussion names a manifest hash made of zeroes. The current manifest has a different
Git blob hash; both remain visible without masking.
Then a stale manifest signature cannot approve publication
Publishing must fail and leave zero public commits. The Publication-manifest marker must
identify the exact manifest being published.
Given an unchanged manifest with no publication sign-off
The prepared manifest is current, but the existing discussion is unrelated. The response and
manifest hash are displayed.
Then approval can request an owner signature for the unchanged manifest
The approval task must succeed and send a POST to the discussions endpoint. The captured
request log shows that request.
Given an approval API that refuses every request
A new candidate path needs approval. The displayed fixture configuration returns HTTP 403
for every API request.
Then approval reports failure when the forge refuses its request
The approval task must return a failure. The card contains its actual error output and the
recorded requests.
Given an approval API that refuses the sign-off thread
A new candidate path needs approval. The fixture API accepts other calls but refuses POST
requests to discussions.
Then approval reports failure when its sign-off thread cannot be
created
The task must fail when creation of the approval thread is refused. The recorded requests
show where the flow stopped.
Given publication tools that record their process arguments
The test wrappers forward to the real tools while recording their arguments. Credentials are
disposable fixture strings.
Then publication keeps both credentials out of process arguments
Publishing must succeed, and neither source nor target token may occur in the recorded
argument list. The displayed searches return zero matches.
Given a publication target URL containing a fixture credential
The target URL deliberately includes a disposable username and token. The setup card shows
this test input.
Then the dry run refuses the credential URL without printing its token
The check must fail, and the command output must not contain the fixture URL token. The
result card displays only actual command output and Git checks.
Given setup whose replacement-token request is refused
The fixture API offers an existing token and refuses creation of a replacement.
Then setup preserves the current token when its replacement fails
Setup must fail without deleting the existing token or enabling publication in .env.dist.
The recorded requests make the absence of token deletion visible.
Given setup whose CI-variable update is refused
The fixture API refuses POST and PUT requests to CI variables.
Then setup preserves the working variable and token after an update
failure
Setup must fail without deleting a working variable or revoking the token still used by CI.
The request log is the evidence for those assertions.
Given setup started from an onboarding branch
The local source is on onboarding. The fixture API exposes main as the project's default
branch.
Then setup enables the discussion gate and schedules the default branch
Setup must succeed, enable only_allow_merge_if_all_discussions_are_resolved, and schedule
main. The captured API request bodies are inspected for both settings.
Given a first source release ready for repeated publication
The source has tag 1.0.0. The next command sequence publishes it, creates a second source
release with identical public bytes, and retries that release.
Then unchanged public bytes retain later releases without duplicating
retries
Both tags must exist and the public history must contain exactly two commits after the
retry. The card shows the real tag list and commit counts at each check.
Given a first source release ready for a later public tag collision
The source has tag 1.0.0. The command sequence publishes it, reserves public tag 1.0.1, then
attempts a different source release with that same tag.
Then a conflicting public tag prevents the branch from moving
The second publication must fail and the public main ref must retain its previous commit.
The real ref reads expose that equality.
Given an untagged source commit ready for publication
The source has no tag. The sequence publishes it, adds tag 1.0.0 to that same source commit,
and publishes again.
Then a tag added later points to the existing public commit
The public tag must point to the original public commit and the public history must still
contain exactly one commit. The card displays the real ref and history checks.

● Given — stage ● When — actions ● Then — proofs
